All right, I will tell you what actually happened, and I am not going to make it sound better than it was. In March we were testing two packaging designs, in two cities, and the test had about three weeks to go. That is what we were doing when the competitor announced almost exactly our product, on the ninth. Two days later we decided to move the launch forward by six weeks. I still think that was the right decision, and I also think it was the wrong preparation, and both of those things can be true at once. We picked design B because it was the one on the table on the day we had to choose, not because the data told us to. Now, the numbers. Awareness doubled in eight weeks. Doubled. That is the best awareness result this brand has ever had and I am proud of it. And sales in the first month came in forty percent under the plan. Those two numbers are describing the same campaign, and I have spent two months understanding why.

Let me tell you how this looks from where I stand, because it is very simple and nobody in marketing seems to enjoy hearing it. I give a new product shelf space and I give it twelve weeks. If it does not sell in twelve weeks, the space goes to somebody who will sell. That is not personal, that is arithmetic. Now, what happened with your launch. Your advertising was excellent. People were coming into my stores and asking for the product by name in week one, which almost never happens, and the shelf was empty, because the stock was in two states and the campaign was in nine. So they bought the competitor, and here is the part that costs you: they did not come back the following week to check again. You spent the money on the hardest thing, which is making somebody want it, and then you were not there. My advice, and I have given it to four companies this year: roll it out slowly. Two states first. It is better to be small and full than national and empty.
